reviewed: Router V2 and LDO board V2 · edited 10 Nov 2026, 16:08 CST · schematic V33B
readiness: Do not order yet: 11 major items to settle, no blocker
headline: FPGA-LDO Option B (router V2 and LDO board V2, schematic V33B) is the same circuit as Option A with DRC, ERC and parity 0 and correct J5 mating, but it has no blocker and 11 major items, and no order files exist yet. The main problems are the few ground and return contacts at J5 and the GND/AGND reference change of the lanes (LDOB-01, LDOB-02, LDOB-03, LDOB-09), safety of a removable module on a live animal (LDOB-04, LDOB-07, LDOB-08), no stack-up in either board file (LDOB-05), retention and the 30-cycle DF40 rating (LDOB-06), and pours or tracks under the DF40 socket contacts (LDOB-10, LDOB-11). First decide whether Option B is worth its ground, safety and retention costs; if so, add return contacts and a defined plane assignment at J5, move the stimulator pull-downs to the router, and set a JLC stack-up before making order files.

findings.already_known: inputs/ldo_b/V2_record/START_HERE.md (Open: 'J5 returns: 2 GND + 1 AGND for 108 signals'). The reviewer agrees it is a decision that must be made before ordering; the record gives no severity, the reviewer rates it major.
findings.title: J5 has only 2 GND and 1 AGND contacts for 108 single-ended ASIC lines, so return paths are long and shared.
findings.what: Every signal needs a return current path back to its source, normally through a nearby ground pin where it crosses a connector. On Option B the 108 single-ended 1.5 V lines through J5 (88 ASIC outputs, 20 FPGA outputs) share 2 GND contacts and 1 AGND contact: 54 signals per GND contact, or 36 per return contact if AGND is counted, and many signals sit far from any of them. A long, shared return adds inductance, so when many lines switch together the local ground jumps (ground bounce) and lines couple to each other; the most likely failure is a false edge on one of the eight CLK32MHz_Out capture clocks, which switch at the same moment as their data. The same lines already cross the ASIC board's DF40-80 connectors in both options at about 15 signals per return contact, so J5 is roughly 2 to 2.5 times worse than a crossing they already make, and the size of the effect is unknown because the ASIC drive strength and edge rate are not specified.
findings.where: Option B router (J5 DF40C-120DS, bottom) and LDO board (J5 DF40C-120DP, top): GND pins 3 and 65, AGND pin 62; worst signal J5.120 (ASIC5_DATA1). Router: J5.65 reaches the L3 GND plane only through a 3.60 mm x 0.20 mm L6 (B.Cu) track to a via in the J4.46 pad at (100.783, 115.10); J5.3 through a 1.91 mm x 0.15 mm L6 track to a via at (87.383, 117.75).
findings.evidence: J5_pin_map_V4.csv and exports/ldo_b_router, exports/ldo_b_ldo pads.csv: 120 pins = 108 signals + 9 rails + 2 GND (3, 65) + 1 AGND (62), 0.4 mm pitch. Pad-centre distance from each signal to the nearest J5 GND pad: LDO board median 4.65 mm, max 11.13 mm (J5.120), 48 signals over 5 mm, 16 over 8 mm; router median 4.77 mm, max 11.23 mm, 51 over 5 mm, 16 over 8 mm; counting AGND the median is 4.40 mm. Comparisons: LDO board J1/J2 carry the same 108 signals on 14 GND (7.7 per contact); router J3/J4 and Option A J3/J4 each carry 58 signals on 2 GND + 2 AGND (29 per GND contact); the ASIC board's DF40C-80 has 61 signal or pass-through pins on 2 DGND + 2 AGND, worst signal about 9 mm from a DGND pin (inputs/asic/J3_pinout__J3_Pinout.csv, J3_pinout__Summary.csv). exports/ldo_b_router/board.json: the two GND tracks above, 3 GND vias, GND pour only on L3 (269.3 mm2). LDO board: a GND via within 0.15 mm of each J5 GND pad, GND planes on L3/L4. Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc sets these lines to LVCMOS15. Estimate, not derived from any file: 40 of 88 ASIC outputs switching together at about 5 mA with 2 ns edges (0.1 A/ns) through an assumed 1-2 nH shared return gives at most 0.1-0.2 V; 1-2 nH is a high-end guess for three contacts in parallel plus vias.
findings.source: Engineering judgement (signal-to-return ratio and loop inductance across a board-to-board connector). AMD DS181 Artix-7 data sheet, LVCMOS15 input thresholds: not checked against the datasheet (docs.amd.com returned 404). DF40 contact inductance: not given in the Hirose catalogue data read.
findings.consequence: Possible capture errors or crosstalk on the 32 MHz data and clock lines, mainly false edges on the CLK32MHz_Out capture clocks. Option B adds this crossing on top of the ASIC-board crossing both options already make; the size of the risk is unknown until the ASIC driver is characterised.
findings.suggested_action: Decide before ordering: add return contacts on J5 (more GND/AGND pins or a small second connector) so no signal is far from a return, or simulate or bench-test the J5 crossing with the ASIC driver and accept it in writing. On the router, add GND vias to L3 at the J5.65 and J5.3 pads.

findings.already_known: inputs/ldo_b/V2_record/START_HERE.md lists the single AGND contact as open; the router lanes referencing AGND are not recorded.
findings.title: All analogue ground current of the four ASIC boards returns to the regulators through one J5 contact, J5.62.
findings.what: AGND is the quiet ground that serves as the reference for the ASICs' analogue circuits. On Option B the only board-level path between the ASIC-side AGND (router L4 plane, J3/J4 pins 42 and 44, all analogue decoupling on the ASIC boards) and the LDO board's regulators is the single contact J5.62, because the router has no AGND-to-GND tie and the ASIC board keeps AGND and DGND apart. The tens of milliamps of analogue rail and stimulation return current make a small shared voltage across that contact, which shifts the reference, REF_VCM, REF_VDD and analogue rails of all eight ASICs together; one contact is also a single point of failure, and if it opens every ASIC analogue ground floats. The current is far below the contact rating, so this is a coupling question, not an overload, and its effect on recordings needs measurement because the ASIC's supply rejection is not specified.
findings.where: J5.62 (AGND) on the router (99.983, 121.74, B.Cu) and the LDO board (99.983, 121.555). Router AGND net (12 pads: J3.42/44, J4.42/44, C51, C53-C57, R6, J5.62) on the L4 (In3.Cu) pour; GND on the L3 (In2.Cu) pour. LDO board: NT1 GND-AGND net tie, bottom, (100.58, 126.81); regulator ground pins of U2, U4-U10 on AGND, U3 (VDD_ADC) and U1 on GND.
findings.evidence: exports/ldo_b_router and exports/ldo_b_ldo pads.csv: J5.62 is the only AGND pad on J5; GND on J5.3 and J5.65. Router zones.csv: GND L3 269.33 mm2, AGND L4 269.81 mm2, one piece each; parts.csv: no router part bridges GND and AGND. exports/asic netlist: /AGND and /DGND are separate, joined by no part other than J3, J4 and the dies. Current from inputs/asic/J3_pinout__Power_Budget.csv x 4 boards: VDD_FE 18.1 mA, VDD_DRIVER 6.0 mA, VDD_CGEN under 0.4 mA, plus VDD_ADC 16.7 mA (decoupled to AGND on the ASIC board) and DVDD 5.6 mA if each returns on AGND; stimulation adds at most about 8 mA at a time, because current flowing from VDD10 to VSS10 does not pass through ground. The re-checks put the total at about 32-49 mA, depending on the undocumented AGND/DGND split inside the ASIC: 3-4.4 mV across the 90 mOhm maximum contact resistance. A 2 mA stimulation step on four boards gives 8 mA x 90 mOhm = 0.72 mV. Option A: J3/J4 pins 42/44 go straight into its own L2 AGND plane (546 mm2), with NT1 on the same board (exports/ldo_a).
findings.source: Hirose DF40 series catalogue, product specifications: contact resistance 90 mOhm max (at 1 mA), rated current 0.25 A for the 120-position part; read from distributor-hosted copies of the Hirose datasheet, as https://www.hirose.com/en/product/pr/df40/ returned 403. Engineering judgement for shared-impedance coupling.
findings.consequence: Stimulation steps and supply-current changes appear as a common shift, under 1 mV worst case, on the analogue reference of every ASIC, more than on Option A; whether that matters depends on the ASIC's unspecified supply and common-mode rejection. A failed J5.62 contact would leave all ASIC analogue grounds floating.
findings.suggested_action: Before ordering, give AGND several J5 contacts spread along the connector, decided together with the J5 return-pin question; then measure AGND noise on the first build.

findings.already_known: The router record (inputs/ldo_b/history/21_.../START_HERE.md) notes 'AGND plane on L4, GND on L3: my choice' without the return-path effect. Related but separate: the J5 return-pin count (2 GND + 1 AGND), open in the V2 record.
findings.title: 89 of 108 Option B lanes run over AGND on one board and GND on the other, pushing digital return into AGND.
findings.what: A fast signal's return current flows in the plane right next to its track. On the router, lanes on L5 and L6 lie over the L4 AGND plane and lanes on L1 and L2 over the L3 GND plane; on the LDO board, L1 lanes lie over the L2 AGND plane and L2/L5 lanes over GND, so 89 of the 108 lanes through J5 spend part of their length over AGND and part over GND. Their return current must change ground net at layer-change vias inside each board and at the far ends: at J1/J2, where the Frontend side is GND only, and at router J3/J4, where AGND meets the ASIC board's AGND pins instead of its digital ground (DGND). The slow part of that current can cross only through NT1, a net tie (a deliberate small copper bridge between two nets) on the LDO board, and the fast edge part crosses through the capacitance between the adjacent GND and AGND planes, which is not a low-impedance path; either way digital switching current lands on AGND, the recording reference.
findings.where: Router: L5 (In4.Cu, 25 signal nets) and L6 (B.Cu, 32 signal nets) over L4 AGND; L1/L2 over L3 GND. LDO board: L1 over L2 AGND; L2/L5 over L3/L4 GND. NT1 (NetTie-2_SMD_Pad0.5mm, 0.5 x 1.0 mm bridge) on the LDO board underside at (100.58, 126.81). J5 GND pins 3 and 65, AGND pin 62. ASIC board J3/J4: AGND pins 42/44, DGND pins 46/48.
findings.evidence: board.json lane copper: router L1 300, L2 255, L5 231, L6 278 mm, so 509 mm references AGND and 555 mm GND; LDO board L1 382 mm (357 mm over filled L2 AGND), L2 338 mm, L5 989 mm. Per-lane majority reference: 57 lanes over AGND on one board and GND on the other, 32 the reverse, 19 over GND on both (both re-checks agree on these counts). One re-check traced the 57 as the 44 ASIC1-4 lanes (router J4) plus 13 shared lanes, over AGND on the LDO board's L1 and GND on the router, and the 32 as 31 ASIC5-8 lanes plus STIM_CHB, the reverse; the original finding had these directions swapped. The 19 GND-only lanes include 10 of the 11 ASIC6 lanes. NT1 is the only GND-AGND joint on either board; its AGND side reaches the L2 plane through 17.22 mm of L6/L5 track and a microvia plus buried-via chain. Neither B board file has a stack-up block; with Option A's JLC stack (JLCH061611Y1-1078) the router L3-L4 plane pair would be about 13 pF (about 380 Ohm at 32 MHz) and the LDO board L2-L3 pair about 120 pF. exports/asic netlist: /AGND and /DGND are separate nets.
findings.source: Engineering judgement (return current follows the adjacent reference plane; a change of reference net needs a nearby low-impedance path between the nets). inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md: the historical FPC carried the 23 signals with 27 DGND conductors and no AGND.
findings.consequence: Digital switching current from up to 89 lanes, 32 MHz clocks among them, is injected into AGND and into the ASIC boards' AGND pins, raising noise on the recording ground and crosstalk between lanes; nothing is measured, so the size is unknown. Changing the plane assignment after fabrication costs a spin of both boards.
findings.suggested_action: Before ordering, choose one ground strategy for the lane field, for example swap the router's L3/L4 nets so L5/L6 lanes reference GND and re-reference the LDO board's L1 lanes to GND; then recheck against the J5 return-pin count.

findings.title: Nothing tells the FPGA the ASIC rails are up, so a live mate can drive unpowered ASIC pins, in either option.
findings.what: The ASIC rail regulators on the LDO board are switched on by a local resistor-capacitor delay, their power-good (PG) outputs are unconnected and there is no presence pin, so the Frontend FPGA cannot tell whether the ASIC rails are up. If a connector carrying the 20 FPGA-to-ASIC outputs is mated while the HDMI cable is live, those outputs can drive unpowered ASIC pins and push current into the ASIC's unpowered supplies through its input protection (back-powering). Option A has the identical circuit, so this is not new to Option B: a live J1/J2 mate gives the full delay window in either option, while at Option B's recorded unplug point, J5, the LDO board is already powered and the exposure is only contact order during a rocking mate, with 44 signal pins more than 5 mm from any return contact. The files cannot settle whether this harms the ASIC: that needs the ASIC designer's powered-off and input-clamp limits (ASIC reference item U03) and a recorded rule on whether boards are ever mated live.
findings.where: LDO board (same in Option A): EN_ASIC_RAILS = R1 10 k from VIN_3V3, C3 4.7 uF, TP4, U1 SHDN, U2-U10 EN; PG pins U2.4, U6.4, U8.4, U9.4, U10.4 unconnected; PGFB tied to VIN_3V3 or STIM_PRE. FPGA-driven J5 pins: board clocks 4 and 27, SPI clocks 63 and 64, STIM SPI 20/22/43/45/54/56/58/59, shared controls 61/66/67/69/115/116/117/119. J5 returns: GND 3 and 65, AGND 62. Spare pins J1.29-49 (13 unconnected) on both the LDO board and the Frontend.
findings.evidence: exports/ldo_b_ldo/netlist.xml and pads.csv: EN_ASIC_RAILS reaches no pin of J1, J2 or J5; time constant 10 k x 4.7 uF = 47 ms, roughly 15-22 ms to the enable thresholds (thresholds not checked against the datasheet), then soft start. exports/ldo_a: identical R1/C3 circuit and unconnected PG pins. Twenty FPGA-driven nets from inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_XEM8305_23_Signal_Map.csv directions applied to J5_pin_map_V4.csv (Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc sets them to LVCMOS15 but gives no direction). J5 pad distances: 44 signal pins more than 5 mm from a return (26-39 and 88, 90-120), up to 11.13 mm. R2-R5 and R16-R18 (10 k to GND) and R19 (10 k to ASIC_DVDD) hold lines only while the FPGA is not driving. Frontend PUDC_B (U1.J18) is pulled high through R25 470 Ohm, so FPGA I/Os float during configuration and a cold power-up with everything mated is not exposed. exports/hdmi: PORT_ENABLE ties U701-U708 EN together, so one port's power cannot be switched off from the host. Weekly deck record: Option B unplugs the LDO board at J5; Option A assumes the Frontend unplugs from J1/J2. No record states a mating procedure.
findings.source: inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md section 10, open item U03 (ASIC powered-off and input-clamp limits absent). LT3042/LT3094 PG, PGFB and EN thresholds: not checked against the datasheet (analog.com fetch timed out). Hirose DF40 hot-plug rating: none found; that DF40 contacts have no make-first length is from memory. Engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: Possible latch-up or damage of the irreplaceable wire-bonded ASICs, or an undefined ASIC state, after a live mate in either option.
findings.suggested_action: Record a 'cable last on, first off' handling rule and ask the ASIC designer for the powered-off input limits. If live mating must be allowed, route a rail-good or presence line to a spare J1 pin on both the LDO board and the Frontend, with a route to an FPGA ball; PG as wired does not report the output rails.

findings.already_known: inputs/ldo_b/V2_record/START_HERE.md lists 'JLC HDI capability' and 'fab files not made' as open; the missing stack-up and the router's different via structure are not named. inputs/ldo_b/history/21_FPGA_LDO_B_Router_Layout_V1/START_HERE.md and 20_.../START_HERE.md note 'Via-in-pad on J5 ... needs filled and capped vias; JLC HDI capability not confirmed'. findings.title: Neither Option B board file names a JLC stack-up, so the 0.10 mm laser vias are not tied to a valid template.
findings.what: A stack-up is the list of copper and insulating layers, with thicknesses, that the factory builds. Both Option B board files carry only KiCad's generic 1.6 mm thickness and no stack-up block, while Option A V12 names JLC template JLCH061611Y1-1078; the B boards were built from Option A V11, before that template was added. JLC's laser microvias (0.10 mm holes) need the outer prepreg (the insulating bonding layer under the outer copper) to be no thicker than the hole, and some of JLC's own general-use templates break that rule, so a template must be named before ordering. The router's via set (laser L1-L2 and L5-L6, through vias, no buried vias) is a standard JLC structure, and the through vias in the DF40 pads rely on epoxy fill and capping, which JLC lists as the default for six-layer boards but which should still be written in the order note, as Option A did.
findings.where: boards/ldo_b_router/FPGA_LDO_B_Router_Layout_V2.kicad_pcb and boards/ldo_b_ldo/FPGA_LDO_B_LDO_Layout_V2.kicad_pcb (thickness 1.6, no stack-up block). Through vias in DF40 pads: router J3 22, J4 22, J5 60 (104); LDO board J5 64.

findings.consequence: An order that picks a wrong general-use template, such as a 2116 stack, would break JLC's laser-via depth rule and be refused or re-engineered. Leaving the via fill out of the order note leaves the J5 solder joints dependent on JLC's default.
findings.suggested_action: Name a JLC template in each B board file and its order note (JLCH061611Y1-1078 for the LDO board, a 1078-prepreg template such as JLCH061611N1-1078A for the router) and request filled, capped via-in-pad in the order note, as Option A V12 did.

findings.title: Option B's plug-in module is held to the head only by the J5 DF40 pair, which is rated for 30 mating cycles.
findings.what: Neither Option B board has any drilled hole, so there is no screw, standoff or clip. The only mechanical link between the removable module (the LDO board with the Frontend, the HDMI plug and the cable load) and the part that stays on the head (the router with four ASIC boards) is the J5 DF40C-120 pair, while Hirose asks for another form of board support and rates the DF40 for 30 mating cycles. Per the project record the LDO board and Frontend come off together, so a routine removal uses one cycle on J5 only; the worn half is the router's DF40C-120DS socket, which stays on the head with the ASIC boards, and removal once per session would use the rating in about a month. The missing holes are not specific to Option B: Option A, the Frontend and the ASIC board have none either, so retention is a decision for the whole head stack.
findings.where: Router J5 DF40C-120DS (bottom, 99.783, 120.2), J3 DF40C-80DP, J4 DF40C-80DS; LDO board J5 DF40C-120DP (top), J1/J2 DF40C-70DP mated to Frontend J1/J2 DF40C-70DS. Router outline 27.9 x 12.62 mm, LDO board 27.9 x 35.30 mm; the ASIC boards reach about 10.3 mm past the router's north edge.

Records: inputs/notes/fpga-ldo-v14.md says the router stays on, the LDO + Frontend module is removable and needs retention; the V2 record's open list has no retention item.

findings.suggested_action: Before the B order, decide how often the module will be removed and what holds it to the head (holes and standoffs, a housing clamp or adhesive), and add holes or keep-outs if needed; if removal will exceed about 30 cycles, choose a higher-cycle connector for J5.

findings.title: The stimulator pull-downs sit on the removable LDO board, so a module lifted at one end of J5 floats them.
findings.what: In Option B, the only resistors that hold the shared stimulator controls (STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CHB, STIM_CLK) low, and the reset/control pulls R16-R19, are on the plug-in LDO board. The router and the ASIC boards have no pull on these nets. The four STIM contacts are at the east end of J5, while every rail and ground contact is further west, so a module seated at the west end and lifted about 0.5-0.7 mm at the east end keeps all eight ASICs powered while their stimulator inputs float (are connected to nothing). The 120-position DF40 has no lock and neither Option B board has a screw or mounting hole, so an incompletely seated module can stay in this state.
findings.where: Router J5 (DF40C-120DS, bottom, centre 99.783, 120.2): STIM_EN J5.115 and STIM_CHB J5.116 (x 110.783), STIM_CLK J5.117 (x 111.183), STIM_START J5.119 (x 111.583), sharing the last three columns with ASIC5_DATA2 J5.118 and ASIC5_DATA1 J5.120. findings.title: Nothing on the head protects ASIC pins at router J5 from static discharge, and no mating procedure exists.
findings.what: ESD (electrostatic discharge) is the spark of static charge from a hand, tool or module into a pin. With the module off, the router and ASIC boards float, tied to the animal only through the ASIC dies and AGND, so whichever J5 contact touches first takes the discharge. The ASIC's ESD rating is not recorded, and no handling procedure or exposed ground touch pad exists; whether to add one is a decision to make before ordering.

findings.title: J5 has three return contacts for 80 ASIC outputs, so data bursts may put a double-crossing step on CLK32.
findings.what: Return current is the current that flows back to the driver through ground; at J5 every ASIC output shares two GND contacts and one AGND contact. When many outputs switch together, that shared current through the contacts' inductance induces a voltage on the quiet CLK32 lines. A model shows this can put a ledge (a flat, non-monotonic step) inside the LVCMOS15 input threshold band of the clock edge, which can make the FPGA input cross its threshold twice and slip a bit. The size depends on the ASIC output edge rate and drive strength, which are unknown, so the files cannot settle this; a CLK32 measurement on a first article with a pseudo-random data pattern would.

findings.title: Mating the LDO board to a powered Frontend dips its 3.3 V rail to about 2.2-2.4 V, below the bucks minimum.
findings.what: The LDO board has about 61 uF of uncharged ceramic capacitance on VIN_3V3 and no inrush limit. If it is mated to a Frontend that is already powered, that capacitance charges from the Frontend's VIN_3V3 rail in a few microseconds, faster than the Frontend regulator U16 can respond, and the shared rail dips to about 2.2-2.4 V. That is below the 2.75 V recommended input minimum of the Frontend's MPM3833C buck modules, but above their typical undervoltage-lockout (UVLO, the voltage where a regulator shuts off) of about 2.1 V, so an FPGA reset is possible with worst-case parts but not likely. In Option B J1/J2 is mated once, unpowered, at assembly, so the realistic exposure is bring-up.

findings.title: Five LDO-board regulators reach their ground plane only through 10-18 mm of thin bottom-layer track.
findings.what: U2, U6 and U8 have vias in their exposed (thermal) pads that reach the ground planes in 0.63 mm. The north-row regulators U3, U4, U5, U9 and U10 do not: their grounds run through 10-18 mm of 0.12-0.30 mm L6 track to two microvia plus buried-via chains before reaching the L2 AGND plane (U3 reaches the GND planes the same way). findings.title: Three router clock lanes run 10-15 mm at a 0.10 mm gap between two switching lines, below good practice.
findings.what: Crosstalk is noise coupled from a switching line into its neighbour. On the router, the ASIC1 and ASIC5 32 MHz clocks and STIM_CLK each run with a switching line 0.10 mm away on both sides, while their ground plane is two layers down (about 0.30 mm, assuming Option A's JLC stack because the router file has no stack-up). Good practice keeps a clock at least 2-3 dielectric heights from switching lines; here the gap is about one third of a height. Modelled noise stays below the FPGA's input margin in every case, and the ASIC launches its data near the clock's rising edge, so this eats margin rather than causing a likely failure; the real risk is only together with the J5 return-bounce finding.

Router L6 ASIC1_CLK32MHz_Out (J4.45 to J5.111) between ASIC1_DATA5 and ASIC1_SYNC, y 113.38 x 100.98-108.78. Router L6 STIM_CLK_SHARED between STIM_EN_SHARED and STIM_START_SHARED, y 112.78 x 102.58-109.38. Shorter runs: ASIC4 CLK32 (L6, 3.6 mm), BOARD1_SPI_CLK (L5, 3.2 mm), BOARD3_SPI_CLK (L2, 2.8 mm).

findings.title: The CLKH clock to the lower ASIC pair runs 11 mm beside two ASIC outputs whose crosstalk lands at its input.
findings.what: BOARD1_CLK carries CLKH, the FPGA's 32 MHz clock, to the lower ASIC pair. On the LDO board it runs between ASIC4_DATA1 and ASIC2_READ, both driven from the ASIC end. Near-end (backward) crosstalk from a line driven at the far end appears at the ASIC end, which is the clock's receiver, and the unterminated input doubles it there. The files cannot settle whether this matters, because the ASIC's input thresholds and hysteresis are not documented; the ASIC designer's figures for them would.
findings.where: LDO board V2: BOARD1_CLK on L5 (x 94.18, y 122.45-134.01), 0.25 mm from ASIC4_DATA1 (11.6 mm) and ASIC2_READ (11.2 mm); on L2 (y 134.01, x 89.9-94.18), 0.30 mm from both for about 4 mm. Router V2 L5: 0.30 mm from ASIC2_READ for 6.46 mm. Router J4.7 and J5.27 = BOARD1_CLK; ASIC connector pin 7 = CLKH.
findings.evidence: Track dump of the refilled LDO and router boards: LDO L5 neighbours ASIC4_DATA1 0.25 mm for 11.58 mm, ASIC2_READ 0.25 mm for 11.15 mm; L2 both at 0.30 mm for 4.0-4.3 mm; router L5 ASIC2_READ 0.30 mm for 6.46 mm. exports/ldo_b_router/pads.csv: J4.7 and J5.27 = /BOARD1_CLK; inputs/asic/J3_pinout__J3_Pinout.csv pin 7 = CLKH. Time-domain peak at the ASIC end, both neighbours switching, 25 ohm: +99/-115 mV at 1 ns edges, +163/-177 mV at 0.5 ns, of which the LDO board contributes 134-144 mV; the ASIC-board part of the path is not included. Re-check short-line estimate (Kb 0.089, 2TD about 145 ps, 0.5 ns edge, doubled, two neighbours): about 150 mV plus the router part.
findings.source: ASIC_REFERENCE.md section 3 (controller supplies CLKH) and U03 (ASIC VIH/VIL not given); engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: If the ASIC clock input has a narrow margin or no hysteresis, READ and DATA activity could add false edges to CLKH and shift the ASIC's frame counting.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer for the input thresholds and hysteresis of CLKH, SPI_CLK and STIM_CLK. If none are available, open the gap around BOARD1_CLK on LDO-board L5 to 0.5 mm.

findings.title: The Frontend and the FPGA-LDO board are joined by two mated DF40 pairs, where Hirose advises only one.
findings.what: Hirose's DF40 drawing asks designers not to use more than one mated connector pair between two stacked (sandwiched) boards, because misalignment between the pairs can break connectors during or after mating. findings.title: Seven clock segments run directly over or under another signal on the next layer, only 0.071 mm away.
findings.what: On the router, layers L1/L2 and L5/L6 have no plane between them, and the same holds for L1/L2 on the LDO board. Where a trace on one layer sits directly on top of a trace on the next layer (broadside coupling), the coupling is strong: the backward coupling coefficient Kb, the fraction of the aggressor's edge that appears on the victim, is about 0.25 to 0.32. The overlaps are only 1.4 to 2.3 mm long, so each adds at most a few tens of millivolts. For the CLK32 pairs, which run in the same direction as the data they overlap, the noise reaches the receiver only after a partial reflection at the ASIC driver, so about 15 to 25 mV is more likely than the doubled upper bound.
findings.where: Router: ASIC2 CLK32 (L5) under ASIC4 CLK32 (L6), 1.5 to 1.6 mm; ASIC5 CLK32 (L1) over ASIC5_DATA2, 1.36 mm; BOARD1_SPI_CLK (L5) under ASIC3_DATA7, 1.78 mm; BOARD3_SPI_CLK (L2) under ASIC7_DATA7, 1.97 mm. LDO board: ASIC3 CLK32 (L2) under ASIC7_DATA8, 2.29 mm; ASIC5 CLK32 (L1) over ASIC5_DATA4, 1.44 mm; ASIC7 CLK32 (L1) over ASIC3_DATA8, 1.39 mm.
findings.evidence: Overlap lengths from board.json (exports/ldo_b_router, exports/ldo_b_ldo), counting adjacent-layer tracks whose centrelines lie within the sum of half-widths, sampled every 0.01 mm; the re-check reproduced every length within 0.05 mm.
